title: Week 1 — From a wave to an evoked response

sessions.title: Sampling: turning a smooth signal into numbers

warmup.q: A recording lasts 2 seconds at 1000 Hz. How many samples does it contain?

options.why: That is the number of samples in 1 second.
Right: 1000 samples per second × 2 seconds.
That would be 2 s at 250 Hz.
That would be 1 sample per second.

warmup.explain: Number of samples = duration × sampling rate.

warmup.q: Inside the computer, one iEEG channel is stored as…

options.why: Computers can only store a finite list of numbers, not a truly continuous curve.

options.t: a list of voltage values, one per sample time
options.why: Right: a time series. The curve you see is drawn by joining these points.
Frequencies come later, from analysis (e.g. Fourier). The raw data is voltage over time.
The display is drawn from numbers; the data itself is numbers.

warmup.explain: Raw data = voltage values at regular time points.

lesson.title: Sampling
simple: The voltage at an electrode changes smoothly all the time. A computer cannot store "all the time", so it takes snapshots: it measures the voltage at regular moments. Each snapshot is a sample.
The sampling rate (written fs) is how many snapshots per second, in hertz (Hz). 1000 Hz = 1000 samples per second = one sample every 1 ms. In general: time between samples = 1 / fs.
Play with the slider. With many samples, the dots trace the wave well. With too few, the dots join into a slower wave that is not really there. This fake slow wave is called aliasing.
lesson.precise: To represent a frequency f without aliasing, you need fs > 2f. The limit fs/2 is the Nyquist frequency. Frequencies above it do not disappear: they fold back to lower frequencies. That is why recording systems apply a low-pass (anti-aliasing) filter before sampling.
lesson.takeaway: Sampling rate = snapshots per second. Too few snapshots create fake slow waves (aliasing).

practice.q: Predict, then check with the slider (set fs to 8 Hz). A 6 Hz wave sampled at 8 Hz: what frequency do the dots appear to show?

options.why: 8 Hz sampling is less than 2 × 6 = 12 Hz, so 6 Hz cannot be shown correctly.
Right: the wave folds back to fs − f = 8 − 6 = 2 Hz.
The sampling rate itself never appears as a wave in the data.
Sampled data cannot show anything above fs/2 = 4 Hz.

practice.explain: When f is between fs/2 and fs, the alias appears at fs − f.

practice.q: Your iEEG system samples at 512 Hz. What is the highest frequency you can analyse, in principle?

options.why: You need more than 2 samples per cycle, so the limit is half of 512.
Sampling never lets you see above the sampling rate.
Right: the Nyquist frequency is 512 / 2 = 256 Hz.
That is a comfortable safe zone (fs/4), but not the theoretical limit.

practice.explain: Nyquist = fs / 2. In practice, stay a bit below it.

practice.q: Spot the error. A student writes: "We sampled at 250 Hz, so we can study high-gamma activity (70–150 Hz)." What is wrong?

options.why: The rule compares the frequency to fs/2, not to fs.

options.t: Part of the band (above 125 Hz) is above the Nyquist frequency
options.why: Right: fs/2 = 125 Hz, so 125–150 Hz cannot be represented.

options.t: High gamma cannot be recorded with iEEG
options.why: iEEG is actually very good for high gamma; the problem is the sampling rate.

options.t: The sampling rate should be exactly 150 Hz
options.why: Sampling at 150 Hz would make it worse: the limit would be 75 Hz.

practice.explain: Check every frequency of interest against fs/2, ideally with margin.

english.text: Signals were sampled at 1 kHz and subsequently downsampled to 500 Hz, which, notwithstanding a modest loss of high-frequency content, was deemed sufficient for the analyses reported here.

q.q: Which phrase shows that this is the authors' judgment, not a proven fact?

options.why: This just describes what was done, in which order.
Right: "to deem" = to judge. The authors decided it was enough.
This is a factual description of the recording.
This only points to the analyses in the paper.

q.explain: "Deemed" signals an evaluation by the authors. A reviewer could disagree.

q.q: "Notwithstanding a modest loss of high-frequency content" means…

options.why: The phrase admits there was a loss.
Right: notwithstanding = despite.

options.t: in order to lose high frequencies
options.why: The loss is a side effect, not the goal.

options.t: except for high frequencies, nothing changed
options.why: Close, but the key meaning is the concession: "despite".

q.explain: Notwithstanding X = despite X. The authors admit a cost, then defend their choice.

english.note: Link to today: at 500 Hz, the Nyquist frequency is 250 Hz, so activity above 250 Hz is lost. That is the "high-frequency content".

explain.q: In your own words: what is the sampling rate, and what goes wrong if it is too low? (2–4 sentences)

sessions.title: Frequency, amplitude, phase: anatomy of a sine wave

warmup.q: At 2000 Hz, how much time passes between two samples?

options.why: That is the gap at 500 Hz.
That is the gap at 50 Hz.
That is 0.5 Hz.

warmup.q: At fs = 1000 Hz, what is the Nyquist frequency?

options.why: That is the sampling rate itself.
The Nyquist frequency is half the sampling rate, not double.
Right: fs / 2.
That is fs/4.

lesson.title: The sine wave
simple: A sine wave is the simplest rhythm: it goes up and down smoothly and regularly. Three numbers describe it completely.
Frequency (Hz): how many full cycles per second. Period: how long one cycle lasts. They are linked: period = 1 / frequency. 10 Hz → 100 ms per cycle.
Amplitude: how high the peaks are (in µV for brain signals). Phase: where in its cycle the wave is at time 0 (in degrees, 0–360°). A 180° shift flips the wave upside down.
Brain rhythms are named by frequency: delta (below 4 Hz), theta (4–8), alpha (8–12), beta (about 13–30), gamma (above 30). Use the sliders to see each one.
lesson.precise: Band limits differ slightly between papers (check each paper's methods). Real brain rhythms are not perfect sines: they come in bursts, drift in frequency, and can have non-sinusoidal shapes. Sines are the building blocks used for analysis, not a literal description of neurons.
lesson.takeaway: Frequency = speed, amplitude = height, phase = starting point. Period = 1 / frequency.

practice.q: Look at the figure. How many full cycles happen in 1 second? So what is the frequency?

options.why: Count the peaks between 0 and 1000 ms: there are more than 2.
Right: 4 peaks (4 full cycles) in 1000 ms.
You may have counted peaks and troughs. A cycle = one peak + one trough.
250 is the period in ms (1000/4), not the frequency.

practice.explain: Count full cycles in 1 s. Careful not to count peaks and troughs separately.

practice.q: A wave completes 5 full cycles in 500 ms. What is its frequency?

options.why: 5 cycles in half a second = 10 cycles in a full second.
Right: 5 cycles / 0.5 s = 10 Hz (alpha range).
100 is the period in ms (500/5), not the frequency.
That would be 5 cycles in 2 s.

practice.explain: Frequency = cycles / seconds. Convert ms to s first.

practice.q: What is the period of a 40 Hz gamma oscillation?

options.why: That is the period of a 25 Hz wave.
Right: 1000 ms / 40 = 25 ms.
That is the period of a 250 Hz wave.
That is the period of a 2.5 Hz wave.

practice.q: Predict, then test with the phase slider. Two 10 Hz waves with the same amplitude, one shifted by 180°. How do they look side by side?

options.why: Identical waves have a 0° (or 360°) shift.

options.t: Mirror images: one is at a peak when the other is at a trough
options.why: Right: 180° is half a cycle, which flips the wave.
Phase changes timing, not frequency.
Phase does not change amplitude.

practice.explain: 180° = half a cycle = upside-down version of the same wave.

english.text: Increased alpha-band power over occipital sites may reflect, at least in part, a functional inhibition of task-irrelevant regions.

options.why: These describe the observation, not the strength of the claim.
Right: "may" = possibly; "at least in part" = maybe not the whole explanation.
These describe the proposed mechanism; they don't weaken it.
Compare with "reflects inhibition": the original is clearly weaker.

q.explain: Hedges show how sure the authors are. Here: a plausible interpretation, not a demonstration.

q.q: Which part is the observation, and which is the interpretation?

options.t: Observation: inhibition of regions. Interpretation: alpha power.
options.why: Reversed: power is measured; inhibition is inferred.

options.t: Observation: more alpha power over occipital sites. Interpretation: functional inhibition.
options.why: Right: you can measure power; "inhibition" is a hypothesis about what it means.
Inhibition is not directly measured in this sentence.
Increased alpha power is a measurement.

q.explain: Always separate what was measured from what it is said to mean.

english.note: Content note: "alpha = inhibition" is a popular and influential hypothesis, but it is still debated (consensus: alpha power changes with attention; debated: what mechanism it reflects).

explain.q: Explain frequency, amplitude and phase in your own words, with one example from brain signals.

sessions.title: Adding signals: what one electrode really records

warmup.q: What is the period of a 4 Hz wave?

options.why: That is the period of a 250 Hz wave.
That is the period of 40 Hz.
That is the period of 2.5 Hz.

warmup.q: An oscillation at 10 Hz belongs to which band?

options.why: Delta is below 4 Hz.
Theta is about 4–8 Hz.
Right: alpha is about 8–12 Hz.
Gamma is above about 30 Hz.

warmup.explain: Delta < 4 · theta 4–8 · alpha 8–12 · beta ~13–30 · gamma > 30 Hz.

warmup.q: A 6 Hz wave sampled at 8 Hz appears at…

options.why: 8 Hz is below 2 × 6, so 6 Hz can't be shown correctly.
Right: fs − f = 2 Hz (aliasing).
Nothing above fs/2 = 4 Hz can appear.
The wave does not vanish; it folds back.

warmup.explain: Alias at fs − f when f is between fs/2 and fs.

lesson.title: Superposition
simple: An electrode does not listen to one source. It records the sum of everything active nearby, at every time point. Adding signals = adding their values point by point. This is called superposition.
Same frequency, same phase → the waves add up into a bigger wave (constructive interference). Same frequency, opposite phase (180°) → they cancel (destructive).
Different frequencies → a more complex shape, for example a slow wave with fast ripples riding on top. Try it: move the second wave's frequency and phase.
Big idea: complex signals can be built from simple sine waves. Next weeks, we will do the reverse: take a complex signal apart into sines. That is what Fourier analysis does.
lesson.precise: Fourier's theorem: a signal over a finite window can be written as a sum of sines, each with its own frequency, amplitude and phase. For electrodes, each source contributes with a weight that depends on its distance and orientation (volume conduction), so the sum is weighted, not equal.
lesson.takeaway: One electrode = sum of many sources. Sums can grow, cancel, or make complex shapes.

practice.q: Predict: a 5 Hz wave + another 5 Hz wave, same amplitude, same phase. What is the sum?

options.why: Adding does not change the frequency of identical waves.

options.t: A 5 Hz wave with twice the amplitude
options.why: Right: constructive interference.
That happens with opposite phases (180°).
Adding cannot slow the wave down here.

practice.q: A large 4 Hz wave + a small 40 Hz wave. What does the sum look like?

options.why: Frequencies are not averaged: both components remain.

options.t: A slow wave with small fast ripples on top
options.why: Right: the slow wave sets the shape, the fast one adds wiggles.
Different frequencies cannot cancel everywhere.

options.t: A fast wave with a small slow ripple
options.why: The 4 Hz wave is the large one here, so it dominates the shape.

practice.explain: Mixtures keep each component; amplitude decides which dominates visually.

practice.q: Predict, then test with the sliders (wave 2 at 6 Hz, amplitude 1). 5 Hz + 6 Hz, equal amplitude: what appears?

options.why: Look at the envelope: the size does not stay steady.

options.t: A wave whose size grows and shrinks once per second
options.why: Right: the two waves drift in and out of phase every second ("beats", at 6 − 5 = 1 Hz).
They only cancel at the moments they are in opposite phase.
Frequencies don't simply add.

practice.explain: Close frequencies → beats at the difference frequency.

practice.q: Challenge your links. A student says: "This electrode shows a 4 Hz rhythm with 40 Hz ripples, so both rhythms come from the same neurons." What's the best reply?

options.t: Correct: one electrode = one neural population
options.why: An electrode sums many sources.

options.t: Plausible, but the recording is a sum: the two rhythms could come from different sources. Which evidence supports a common origin?
options.why: Right: co-occurrence in the sum is not evidence of a common source.

options.t: Wrong: 40 Hz can't be recorded with 4 Hz
options.why: Both can be present in the same recording.

options.t: Correct, because 40 is a multiple of 4
options.why: A numerical ratio does not show a shared origin.

practice.explain: Seeing two things together in a sum ≠ one shared cause.

english.text: Figure 2. (A) Simulated signal composed of a 6 Hz and a 40 Hz component. (B) Same signal after the addition of broadband noise. Note that the 40 Hz component, although clearly visible in A, is largely obscured in B.

q.q: Which panel would you look at to check that the signal really contains 40 Hz?

options.why: Right: the caption says the 40 Hz component is clearly visible there.
In B, the 40 Hz component is largely obscured by noise.
The caption says A shows it clearly.
The point of the figure is that they differ.

q.explain: Captions tell you which panel carries which point.

q.q: "Largely obscured" means the 40 Hz component in B is…

options.why: "Largely" means mostly, not completely; and noise hides, it doesn't remove.
Right: obscured = hidden; largely = mostly.
"Largely" is about degree, not size.
Obscured means the opposite.

q.explain: The component is still in the data; noise just hides it. Remember this for next session!

english.note: "Broadband noise" = noise spread over many frequencies (not a single peak like line noise).

explain.q: Why can one electrode show a complicated wave even if each source is a simple rhythm? (2–4 sentences)

warmup.q: Two identical 10 Hz waves, shifted by 180°, are added. Result?

options.why: That is for 0° shift.
Right: destructive interference.
Frequency does not change.
Frequency does not change.

warmup.q: You sample at 250 Hz. Time between samples?

options.why: That would be 4 Hz sampling.
That would be 40 Hz sampling.
That would be 2500 Hz sampling.

lesson.title: Noise
simple: Noise is everything in the recording that is not what you want to study: other brain activity, muscle activity, mains electricity (line noise, 50 Hz in Europe), amplifier noise.
Superposition again: recording = signal + noise. The noise doesn't replace the signal; it is added on top and can hide it.
Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR): how big the signal is compared to the noise. High SNR: easy to see. Low SNR: hidden. Move the slider and find the noise level where you can no longer see the wave.
A single-trial evoked response is often smaller than the ongoing background activity, so its SNR is low. Tomorrow: the trick to fix that.
lesson.precise: SNR is usually defined as a ratio of power (amplitude squared), often in decibels: 10·log10(P_signal / P_noise). "Noise" depends on the question: ongoing alpha is noise for an ERP study and signal for an alpha study. Structured noise (like a 50 Hz line) can often be removed by a filter; random broadband noise in the same frequencies as your signal cannot be filtered away.
lesson.takeaway: Recording = signal + noise. SNR = how much the signal stands out.

practice.q: A recording in Grenoble shows a narrow, constant peak at 50 Hz in every channel. Most likely cause?

options.why: A brain rhythm would rarely be exactly 50 Hz, constant, and in every channel.
Right: 50 Hz is the European mains frequency.
Aliasing creates lower, not higher, frequencies.
Muscle noise is broadband (many frequencies), not one narrow peak.

practice.explain: Narrow + constant + everywhere + 50 Hz = line noise.

practice.q: The signal stays the same, but the noise amplitude doubles. The SNR (as an amplitude ratio)…

options.why: More noise makes the ratio smaller, not bigger.
Right: signal / (2 × noise) = half the previous ratio.
The ratio depends on the noise, which changed.
That would be true for a power ratio (amplitude squared), not an amplitude ratio.

practice.explain: Amplitude SNR = signal / noise. (In power: divided by 4. See the precise version.)

practice.q: In a study of evoked potentials, the ongoing alpha rhythm in the background is…

options.t: always signal, because it is brain activity
options.why: Being neural doesn't make it the signal of interest.
Right: noise is defined relative to the question.
An artefact is non-brain or technical; alpha is genuine brain activity.

options.t: impossible to record at the same time
options.why: Both are recorded together and add up.

practice.explain: Signal vs noise is about your question, not about the source.

practice.q: Why do iEEG contacts often show clearer local responses than scalp EEG?

options.why: Sampling rate does not set the SNR of a local response.

options.t: They are close to the source, without skull and scalp spreading the signal
options.why: Right: bigger local signal and less mixing with distant sources.

options.t: There is no noise inside the brain
options.why: Other brain activity is still there and still counts as noise.
iEEG still needs a reference (topic for a later week).

practice.explain: Distance and tissue between source and sensor shape SNR.

english.text: Trials contaminated by artefacts exceeding ±150 µV were excluded, resulting in the rejection of 12% of trials on average (range: 3–27%).

options.why: The numbers are percentages, not trial counts.

options.t: The participant (or recording) with the fewest rejections lost 3%, the one with the most lost 27%
options.why: Right: the range shows the spread behind the 12% average.
An average of 12% fits easily within 3–27%.
The threshold was ±150 µV; the range refers to rejected trials.

q.explain: Averages hide spread. A reader should wonder: does 27% rejection bias that participant's data?

options.t: All trials with amplitude below 150 µV
options.why: Reversed: the threshold catches big values.

options.t: Trials where the artefact went beyond +150 or −150 µV
options.why: Right: "exceeding ±150 µV" = above +150 or below −150.
Rejection was based on a threshold, not random.
Only large artefacts beyond the threshold.

q.explain: "±" = plus or minus: both directions count.

english.note: Spelling: "artefact" (UK) = "artifact" (US). Both are correct; be consistent in your own writing.

explain.q: Define noise and SNR in your own words. Give one example where the same activity is signal in one study and noise in another.

sessions.title: Averaging trials: making the evoked response appear

options.t: Signal only, after the amplifier removes noise
options.why: Amplifiers add some noise; they don't remove it all.

options.t: Signal + noise, added point by point
options.why: Right: superposition.
For our purposes, noise adds; it does not multiply.

options.t: Noise only, the signal is computed later
options.why: The signal is in the recording, hidden among the noise.

warmup.q: Which is a typical source of structured (non-random) noise?

options.why: Right: a fixed, predictable frequency.
That noise is random and broadband.
That's usually the signal of interest.
A sampling rate is a setting, not noise.

warmup.explain: Structured noise has a predictable form, which makes it easier to remove.

lesson.title: Averaging
simple: Problem: one trial's response is hidden in noise. Trick: show the stimulus many times. Cut the recording around each stimulus (each piece is an epoch), align them on stimulus onset (time 0), and average them point by point.
The response is time-locked: same shape, same time on every trial, so it stays. The noise is random: positive on some trials, negative on others, so it cancels out and shrinks.
Rule of thumb: noise in the average shrinks with √N. 4× more trials → noise halves. Use the slider and watch the true response (dashed) appear.
The result is an evoked potential. Its bumps are called deflections. Describe each one by polarity (positive/negative), latency (ms after the stimulus) and amplitude (µV).
lesson.precise: The √N rule assumes noise is independent across trials with zero mean, and the response is identical on every trial. If latency jitters, the average gets smaller and wider. Activity that is not phase-locked to the stimulus (induced oscillations) averages out even if it is real, so you need time-frequency analysis on single trials to see it. The polarity of a deflection also depends on the reference and the electrode's position relative to the source.
lesson.takeaway: Time-locked signal stays, random noise shrinks by √N. Bumps = deflections: polarity, latency, amplitude.

practice.q: You have 25 trials. How many do you need to halve the noise in the average?

options.why: Doubling trials only reduces noise by √2 ≈ 1.4.
Right: 4× more trials → √4 = 2× less noise.
That would divide the noise by 5 compared with 25 trials.
Fewer trials increase the noise in the average.

practice.explain: Noise ∝ 1/√N. To halve it, multiply N by 4.

practice.q: Look at this average of 100 trials (positive up). Describe the first deflection.

options.why: That is the second deflection. Look earlier.
Right: the first clear bump goes down and peaks near 100 ms.
At 0 ms the stimulus just appeared; the response comes later.
With 100 trials, the noise is small enough to see the bumps.

practice.explain: Polarity + latency (+ amplitude) describe a deflection.

practice.q: Predict: the response latency varies randomly by about ±50 ms from trial to trial. The averaged deflection will be…

options.why: Misaligned peaks don't add up perfectly.

options.t: smaller and wider than the single-trial response
options.why: Right: peaks at different times are smeared across time.
Jitter can only blur, not sharpen.
Some overlap remains, so a reduced, broad bump survives.

practice.explain: Latency jitter: the average underestimates the single-trial amplitude.

practice.q: After each stimulus, a gamma burst appears, but at a random phase. In the averaged evoked potential, it…

options.why: Random phase means peaks and troughs cancel across trials.

options.t: mostly disappears, even though it's real
options.why: Right: it is induced, not phase-locked, activity.
Averaging does not change frequency.
Averaging cannot amplify beyond a single trial.

practice.explain: Absence in the average ≠ absence in the brain.

english.text: Although the late component did not reach significance, its topography was consistent with a parietal generator, a possibility that warrants further investigation.

q.q: Do the authors claim that the late component comes from parietal cortex?

options.why: "Consistent with" and "a possibility" are much weaker than a claim.

options.t: No: they say it fits a parietal source, as a possibility to test
options.why: Right: two hedges, "consistent with" and "a possibility".

options.t: No: they say it is not parietal
options.why: They suggest parietal is possible, not excluded.
The sentence says it did not reach significance.
It asks for more work precisely because it is not confirmed.
Right: to warrant = to justify or deserve.
The opposite.
A warrant is also a legal document, but not in this sense.

q.explain: A polite way to say: we don't know yet.

english.note: When you read a "null + interesting" sentence like this, ask: would I believe it if the result went the other way?

explain.q: Explain to a first-year student why averaging 100 trials reveals a response invisible in one trial. Mention one situation where averaging fails.

checkup.title: Week 1 check-up
checkup.intro: About 15–20 minutes, optional. Mixed questions from the whole week, then one longer explanation. Reminder: tap "Backup progress" on the Progress screen and save the code somewhere safe.

options.why: That is 400 Hz.
That is 40 Hz.
That is 4 Hz.
Nyquist is half fs, not double.
That is fs itself.
Right: fs/2.
That is fs/4.

questions.q: A 90 Hz oscillation sampled at 100 Hz (no anti-aliasing filter) appears at…

options.why: 90 Hz is above Nyquist (50 Hz).
Right: 100 − 90 = 10 Hz. A fake alpha-like rhythm!
Nothing above 50 Hz can appear.
It folds back; it is not removed.

questions.explain: Aliasing can create rhythms that look physiological. That's why anti-aliasing filters matter.

questions.q: Period of an 8 Hz theta/alpha-border wave?

options.why: That is 125 Hz.
That is 12.5 Hz.
That is 1.25 Hz.

questions.q: Two sources at the same frequency are recorded by one electrode with opposite phases and equal amplitude. The electrode shows…

options.why: That needs them in phase.

options.t: little or nothing at that frequency
options.why: Right: they cancel. Active sources can be invisible in the sum!
Frequency is unchanged.
An electrode records one summed value per time point.

questions.explain: No signal at an electrode ≠ no activity in the brain.

questions.q: Noise amplitude is halved, signal unchanged. Amplitude SNR…

options.why: Right: signal / (noise/2) = 2 × the old ratio.
Less noise improves the ratio.
The noise changed, so the ratio changes.
That's true for the power ratio, not amplitude.

questions.q: From 16 to 64 trials, noise in the average is…

options.why: Noise follows √N: √64/√16 = 8/4 = 2.
Right.
No rule based on the difference.
More trials do reduce random noise.

questions.q: Which sentence makes the strongest claim?

options.why: "May" + "contribute" = doubly hedged.
"Consistent with" = compatible, not causal.
Right: no hedge, and a causal claim.

options.t: "X is a putative marker of Y."
options.why: "Putative" = assumed, not proven.

questions.explain: Rank claims by verb strength (causes > contributes > is associated with > is consistent with) and hedges.
